subject: Mathematics
topic: Equivalent fractions and comparison of rational numbers
title: Equivalent Fractions and Comparing Rational Numbers
summary: 1 slice of 2 or 4 slices of 8: who ate more pizza? Learn equivalent fractions, the LCM trick for comparing, and why −3/4 > −5/6.

notes.title: 04 – Equivalent Fractions and Comparison of Rational Numbers

keyPoints: Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the **same non-zero number**: the value does not change.
To compare, make the **denominators equal** (use the LCM), then compare numerators.
Cross-multiplication: for a/b and c/d (b, d > 0), compare **a × d** with **b × c**.
For negatives the order flips: **−3/4 > −5/6** (nearer to 0).

blocks.p: Rahul eats 1 of 2 slices; Priya eats 4 of 8 slices of the same pizza. They ate the **same amount**: 1/2 and 4/8 are **equivalent fractions**.

blocks.formula: p/q = (p × m)/(q × m)   for any non-zero m

blocks.alt: Fraction bars for 1/2, 2/4, 3/6 and 4/8 shading the same length
blocks.caption: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8: the shaded length is the same.

list: Write both with a positive denominator.
Find the LCM of the denominators.
Rewrite both with the LCM as denominator.

blocks.caption: With equal pieces, the comparison is easy.

blocks.p: For negative numbers the order reverses. −3/4 = −0.75 sits to the **right** of −5/6 ≈ −0.83 on the number line, nearer to 0, so **−3/4 > −5/6**.

blocks.alt: Number line from -1 to 0 marking -5/6 and -3/4
blocks.caption: The one nearer to 0 is bigger.

quiz.explain: With denominator 12: 3/4 = 9/12 and 5/6 = 10/12; 10/12 is greater, so 5/6 > 3/4.
−3/4 = −0.75 is nearer to 0 than −5/6 ≈ −0.83, so −3/4 is greater.
Cross-multiply: 5 × 24 = 120 and 8 × 15 = 120. Equal products, so they are equivalent.

quiz.q: Adding 1 to both the numerator and denominator of 1/2 gives 2/3. Is 2/3 equivalent to 1/2?
quiz.explain: Adding the same number does not keep the value (1/2 = 0.5, 2/3 ≈ 0.67). Only multiplying or dividing both by the same number does.

simulation.reason: Choosing any two fractions (including negatives) and watching both bars re-cut into LCM pieces, and both points land on a number line, lets students test their own guesses about equivalence and order - exploration a fixed video example cannot give.
simulation.objective: Turn any two fractions into the same-sized pieces and see which is bigger, on bars and on a number line.
instructions: Set the two fractions with the + and − buttons (numerators may be negative).
Press 'Same pieces' to re-cut both bars into LCM pieces.
Read the verdict and check where both fractions sit on the number line.
Try −3/4 against −5/6 to see the order flip.
